title: Rethinking Classifier-Free Guidance for TI2I Flow Matching

paper.title: Rethinking Classifier-Free Guidance for TI2I Flow Matching
paper.abstract: Abstract We study Text-and-Image-to-Image (TI2I) flow matching methods for controllable image editing. In a broader generative modeling context, Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) is established as a key component responsible for high quality outputs. However, we argue that its role in TI2I modeling is poorly understood. Specifically, we make the surprising observation that the CFG mechanism is implicitly harmful for editing in the noisy phase of flow modeling, hindering instruction following and controllability. We propose a simple correction in the early flow steps, enabling a richer alignment-preservation tradeoff at no extra cost. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated on both pixel-space and latent TI2I flows.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Text-and-Image-to-Image (TI2I) editing is the task of modifying a source image according to a text prompt while retaining the source wherever no change is intended. The source image provides the concrete visual instance, including scene, object identity, composition, appearance and incidental details. The prompt instead serves as an instruction specifying how that instance should change. Crucially, a successful edit must apply the requested changes without reopening the rest of the image for synthesis. TI2I editing methods studied in the literature typically adapt pretrained Text-to-Image (T2I) models. These methods are often training-free, so their design space concentrates on inference-time mechanisms ( Kulikov et al., 2025 ; Yang and Ye, 2026 ) . This adaptation paradigm has produced a broad and useful set of techniques but it also inherits limitations from models trained primarily for T2I generation. In parallel, a newer line of systems trains text-and-image-conditioned flows directly for editing ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Black Forest Labs, 2025b ) . These models are increasingly important yet their properties remain comparatively underexplored. In this paper, we study this setting of bespoke TI2I flow matching, rather than editing through adaptation of a T2I generator. Specifically, we focus on the nuance of Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG), which is a central mechanism of modern generative flows ( Ho and Salimans, 2021 ) . In T2I generation, increasing the CFG weight, ω \omega , is commonly understood as improving text alignment at the cost of sample diversity and, at large values, visual naturalness ( Zheng and Lan, 2024 ; Karras et al., 2024 ) . In editing, however, the relevant tradeoff is alignment versus preservation with respect to the source. In that case, we find that CFG produces a poorly shaped guidance tradeoff. That is, small ω \omega weakens instruction following but may not reliably reduce distortion, while large ω \omega is often essential for alignment but tends to amplify unnecessary changes. We identify the source of this inefficiency and attribute it to the well-established and widely adopted recipe of Ho and Salimans (2021) . As demonstrated in Figure 1 , we propose a simple inference-time correction that largely mitigates the issue. Our intervention requires no additional evaluations, leaves the trained model unchanged and recovers a richer set of operating points as ω \omega varies. We show this in two settings. For a controlled analysis, we use a PixelGen ( Ma et al., 2026b ) finetune for pixel-space editing. We then demonstrate our approach in more general editing, benchmarking via Qwen-Image-Edit ( Wu et al., 2025 ) and FLUX.2 ( Black Forest Labs, 2025b ) , representative off-the-shelf latent flows tailored for the task.

sections.heading: 2.2 Text-and-Image-to-Image Modeling
sections.text: TI2I models generate edit candidates conditioned jointly on a source image, 𝒄 img \boldsymbol{c}^{\text{img}} , and a text prompt or instruction 𝒄 txt \boldsymbol{c}^{\text{txt}} . That is, the target distribution here is of the form p ( ⋅ ∣ 𝒄 img , 𝒄 txt ) p(\cdot\mid\boldsymbol{c}^{\text{img}},\boldsymbol{c}^{\text{txt}}) . Unlike T2I generation, which has weaker conditioning, sampling from p ( ⋅ ∣ 𝒄 txt ) p(\cdot\mid\boldsymbol{c}^{\text{txt}}) , TI2I editing requires balancing two competing guiding signals and goals. Namely, adherence to the requested edit and preservation of source content. Most editing methods in the literature do not train TI2I editing models directly. Instead, they adapt pretrained T2I models at inference time, effectively exploiting their strong generative priors while avoiding additional optimization costs ( Meng et al., 2022 ; Rout et al., 2025 ; Kulikov et al., 2025 ; Yang and Ye, 2026 ) . Alternatively, it is also possible to train a generator directly for image editing. Early diffusion-based examples include Brooks et al. (2023) , which learns to follow natural-language editing instructions from paired editing data. More recently, large-scale multimodal flow models have been trained natively with both image and text conditioning, enabling direct modeling of the TI2I distribution ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Black Forest Labs, 2025b ) . Notably, in these systems, the source image enters the model as a first-class conditioning signal. In particular, for flow matching models, conditioning is typically incorporated into the velocity field, 𝒗 𝜽 ​ ( 𝒙 t , t , 𝒄 img , 𝒄 txt ) \boldsymbol{v}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_{t},t,\boldsymbol{c}^{\text{img}},\boldsymbol{c}^{\text{txt}}) , so that the sampling trajectory is jointly determined by the current state, source image and textual instruction.

sections.heading: 3 Methodology
sections.text: Before proceeding with analysis, we summarize our experimental setup. For completeness, we consider both pixel-space and latent-space TI2I models. In particular, pixel-space modeling enables a controlled and more interpretable setup. To this end, we produce a TI2I finetune of PixelGen ( Ma et al., 2026b ) at 512 × 512 512\times 512 resolution. For latent-space modeling, we experiment with Qwen-Image-Edit ( Wu et al., 2025 ) and the FLUX.2 family ( Black Forest Labs, 2025b ) at 256 × 256 256\times 256 , 512 × 512 512\times 512 and 1024 × 1024 1024\times 1024 image resolutions. Throughout the paper, we use synthetic datasets, created by existing foundation models. After quality control, each contains approximately 200 entries. Specifically, we first generate text triplets of source image descriptions, edit instructions and post-edit descriptions via Claude Opus 4.7. Source descriptions are then used to generate source images via FLUX.2. Additionally, for local editing with PixelGen, we constrain the text triplets to describe scenarios where changes are expected to be strictly confined within specific regions in the images. In that case, we use the Segment Anything Model (SAM) of Carion et al. (2026) to automatically obtain corresponding segmentation masks. For latent-space editing with Qwen and FLUX.2, which we found to be significantly more capable, we allow general and challenging triplets to effectively test limitations. Further details on infrastructure, data, model configurations and hyperparameters are given in Appendix A .

sections.heading: 3.3 Early Correction Unlocks a Richer Alignment-Preservation Tradeoff
sections.text: Having introduced early correction, we now turn to evaluation. As discussed in Section 1 , we are interested in quantifying the alignment-preservation tradeoff. We consider various proxies for each axis that are commonly adopted in the literature. Alignment is quantified by comparing the post-edit images with target post-edit descriptions via CLIP similarity ( Radford et al., 2021 ) , PickScore ( Kirstain et al., 2023 ) and HPSv3 ( Ma et al., 2025 ) . Separately, we use the Aesthetics predictor ( Schuhmann, 2022 ) , a no-reference, unconditional human preference proxy operating only on images. For preservation, we compare post-edit images with corresponding source images via PSNR, LPIPS ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) and DINOv2 ( Oquab et al., 2024 ) . We interpret this to mean that our correction alone leads to better localization, effectively approximating the masked oracle. sections.heading: 4 Discussion
sections.text: Figure 9 : We show DINOv2-HPSv3, Aesthetics tradeoffs for the PixelGen, FLUX.2 and Qwen models with different ω \omega and τ \tau . Curves represent fixed ω \omega and form by varying τ \tau , with faint colors given to small values. A positive τ \tau often improves all metrics. We studied CFG in TI2I flows and argued the recipe of Ho and Salimans (2021) is poorly integrated. Our observation is that CFG trains the text-unconditional branch to approximate the mean edit rather than a no-edit flow, so the mechanism responsible for alignment implicitly erodes preservation. We localized this effect to the noisy phase of modeling and proposed an intervention that substitutes a no-edit velocity into the unconditional branch for t < τ t<\tau . It requires no additional evaluations and recovers markedly richer alignment-preservation tradeoffs. We do not present a rule for τ \tau . In practice, however, a uniform choice delivers consistent improvements. Moreover, we note that open TI2I models often do not provide complete information about their development, which may involve post-training we cannot account for. In these cases, we cannot cleanly attribute the success or relative ineffectiveness of our intervention to flow modeling alone. Our findings caution against blind transfer of techniques across tasks. Despite its ubiquity, CFG is not a silver bullet and its naive application is harmful for source preservation in editing. We therefore view our work as an invitation to rethink such recipes. Instead of treating editing as T2I generation with an additional conditioning signal, we argue that TI2I modeling benefits from task-specific context, here a no-edit prior grounding generation to the source, and hope this perspective informs the design of future systems.

sections.heading: Appendix A Experimental Setup
sections.text: We ran inference on Linux machines using RTX Quadro 6000, RTX A5000, H100 GPUs and CUDA 13.0. Benchmarks were generated via Claude Opus 4.7, FLUX.2 [klein] 4B Base ( Black Forest Labs, 2025b ) ( 1024 × 1024 1024\times 1024 , 50 steps, ω = 4 \omega=4 , Euler) and SAM 3 ( Carion et al., 2026 ) , with compositions in Figure 10 . For TI2I editing, which consumed most of our compute budget, we used the Euler solver with 25 steps. Preliminary runs with the recommended 50 steps showed little difference and did not justify the extra cost. Regarding our pixel-space experiments, we finetuned PixelGen-XXL ( Ma et al., 2026b ) ( 512 × 512 512\times 512 , bf16) on NHR-Edit ( Kuprashevich et al., 2026 ) , OmniEdit ( Wei et al., 2025 ) , X2I ( Xiao et al., 2025 ) datasets for TI2I modeling and on Fine-T2I ( Ma et al., 2026a ) for T2I preservation. We used the JiT flow-matching velocity loss from Li and He (2026) and LPIPS, DINOv2, REPA ( Yu et al., 2025 ) regularizers applied similarly to the original PixelGen recipe, gated at t = 0.5 t=0.5 . We additionally applied unconditional T2I regularization and a KL penalty ( β = \beta= 1e-3) against a frozen reference to preserve base generative quality. The model was trained with the AdamW optimizer, a learning rate of 1e-4 and a batch size of 128 for 20k iterations. We note that our adaptation of PixelGen reuses the T2I backbone without introducing any new parameters. In particular, source conditioning is realized through token concatenation, following the Kontext paradigm ( Black Forest Labs, 2025a ) . That is, source images are embedded like the noisy inputs and their tokens are appended to the noisy token sequence inside the transformer. To distinguish them, noisy tokens carry the denoising timestep whereas source tokens are marked as noise-free, i.e., t = 1 t=1 . With this setup, information therefore propagates through the model’s existing joint attention, requiring no adapters or auxiliary encoders.

In a broader generative modeling context, Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) is established as a key component responsible for high quality outputs. However, we argue that its role in TI2I modeling is poorly understood. Specifically, we make the surprising observation that the CFG mechanism is implicitly harmful for editing in the noisy phase of flow modeling, hindering instruction following and controllability. We propose a simple correction in the early flow steps, enabling a richer alignment-preservation tradeoff at no extra cost. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated on both pixel-space and latent TI2I flows. Figure 1 : We propose a simple modification in TI2I flows that substantially improves source preservation while maintaining text alignment. In the examples above, source images are on the left, baseline edits in the middle (we evaluate Qwen, FLUX.2 and PixelGen models) and editing with our correction on the right. 1 Introduction Text-and-Image-to-Image (TI2I) editing is the task of modifying a source image according to a text prompt while retaining the source wherever no change is intended. The source image provides the concrete visual instance, including scene, object identity, composition, appearance and incidental details. The prompt instead serves as an instruction specifying how that instance should change. Crucially, a successful edit must apply the requested changes without reopening the rest of the image for synthesis. TI2I editing methods studied in the literature typically adapt pretrained Text-to-Image (T2I) models. These methods are often training-free, so their design space concentrates on inference-time mechanisms ( Kulikov et al., 2025 ; Yang and Ye, 2026 ) . This adaptation paradigm has produced a broad and useful set of techniques but it also inherits limitations from models trained primarily for T2I generation. In parallel, a newer line of systems trains text-and-image-conditioned flows directly for editing ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Black Forest Labs, 2025b ) . These models are increasingly important yet their properties remain comparatively underexplored. In this paper, we study this setting of bespoke TI2I flow matching, rather than editing through adaptation of a T2I generator. Specifically, we focus on the nuance of Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG), which is a central mechanism of modern generative flows ( Ho and Salimans, 2021 ) . In T2I generation, increasing the CFG weight, ω \omega , is commonly understood as improving text alignment at the cost of sample diversity and, at large values, visual naturalness ( Zheng and Lan, 2024 ; Karras et al., 2024 ) . In editing, however, the relevant tradeoff is alignment versus preservation with respect to the source. In that case, we find that CFG produces a poorly shaped guidance tradeoff. That is, small ω \omega weakens instruction following but may not reliably reduce distortion, while large ω \omega is often essential for alignment but tends to amplify unnecessary changes. We identify the source of this inefficiency and attribute it to the well-established and widely adopted recipe of Ho and Salimans (2021) . As demonstrated in Figure 1 , we propose a simple inference-time correction that largely mitigates the issue. Our intervention requires no additional evaluations, leaves the trained model unchanged and recovers a richer set of operating points as ω \omega varies. We show this in two settings. For a controlled analysis, we use a PixelGen ( Ma et al., 2026b ) finetune for pixel-space editing. We then demonstrate our approach in more general editing, benchmarking via Qwen-Image-Edit ( Wu et al., 2025 ) and FLUX.2 ( Black Forest Labs, 2025b ) , representative off-the-shelf latent flows tailored for the task. 2 Background We give a brief overview of literature on modern generative flows, techniques for TI2I modeling and CFG. 2.1 Flow Matching Flows perform generative modeling through Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs) ( Chen et al., 2018 ) . In practice, this is done by dropping conditioning information during training for a fraction of the iterations, effectively unifying the two flows under a single parameterization. Despite the theoretical elegance of CFG, subtle technical details make it a non-trivial mechanism, with more nuanced dynamics and interpretation than the original motivation suggests ( Zheng and Lan, 2024 ; Karras et al., 2024 ) . Moreover, its design in the presence of multimodal conditioning remains relatively unexplored. 3 Methodology Before proceeding with analysis, we summarize our experimental setup. For completeness, we consider both pixel-space and latent-space TI2I models. In particular, pixel-space modeling enables a controlled and more interpretable setup. To this end, we produce a TI2I finetune of PixelGen ( Ma et al., 2026b ) at 512 × 512 512	imes 512 resolution. For latent-space modeling, we experiment with Qwen-Image-Edit ( Wu et al., 2025 ) and the FLUX.2 family ( Black Forest Labs, 2025b ) at 256 × 256 256	imes 256 , 512 × 512 512	imes 512 and 1024 × 1024 1024	imes 1024 image resolutions. Throughout the paper, we use synthetic datasets, created by existing foundation models. After quality control, each contains approximately 200 entries. Specifically, we first generate text triplets of source image descriptions, edit instructions and post-edit descriptions via Claude Opus 4.7. We studied CFG in TI2I flows and argued the recipe of Ho and Salimans (2021) is poorly integrated. Our observation is that CFG trains the text-unconditional branch to approximate the mean edit rather than a no-edit flow, so the mechanism responsible for alignment implicitly erodes preservation. We localized this effect to the noisy phase of modeling and proposed an intervention that substitutes a no-edit velocity into the unconditional branch for t < τ t<	au . It requires no additional evaluations and recovers markedly richer alignment-preservation tradeoffs. We do not present a rule for τ 	au . In practice, however, a uniform choice delivers consistent improvements. Moreover, we note that open TI2I models often do not provide complete information about their development, which may involve post-training we cannot account for. In these cases, we cannot cleanly attribute the success or relative ineffectiveness of our intervention to flow modeling alone. Our findings caution against blind transfer of techniques across tasks. Despite its ubiquity, CFG is not a silver bullet and its naive application is harmful for source preservation in editing. We therefore view our work as an invitation to rethink such recipes. Instead of treating editing as T2I generation with an additional conditioning signal, we argue that TI2I modeling benefits from task-specific context, here a no-edit prior grounding generation to the source, and hope this perspective informs the design of future systems.
